query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of Hf (~0.5 at%) to a eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of Hf‐rich precipitates at the lamellar and colony boundaries, thereby simultaneously enhancing yield/ultimate tensile strengths and mitigating microcrack propagation to improve room‐temperature tensile ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting abundant internal boundaries that serve as microcrack initiation sites under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating a small amount of Hf (approximately 0.5 at%) during synthesis, followed by conventional thermo-mechanical processing to allow formation of interfacial Hf-rich precipitates.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing following standard casting, rolling, and annealing procedures that yield the characteristic lamellar colony structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Hf-rich phase precipitates that form predominantly at internal boundaries (grain and colony interfaces).
generation.mechanism: The Hf-rich precipitates are expected to act as pinning centers that stabilize the internal boundaries, thereby suppressing microcrack initiation and propagation during tensile deformation while also contributing to precipitation strengthening. This dual effect leads to improved strength without compromising ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline unmofidied eutectic HEA, the Hf-modified alloy should exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with enhanced plastic strain (ductility) during room-temperature tensile tests.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with conventional lamellar colony microstructure, which demonstrates high strength at the expense of room-temperature ductility due to premature brittle fracture from microcrack propagation.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected when Hf addition is precisely controlled (~0.5 at%) and processing conditions allow uniform formation of Hf-rich precipitates at the critical boundaries. Deviations in Hf concentration or processing may lead to nonuniform precipitate distribution or embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: While high-temperature studies suggest Hf can be beneficial via precipitation strengthening and boundary pinning, it remains uncertain whether these effects translate with the same magnitude and mechanisms to room-temperature conditions in eutectic HEAs.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples using identical casting, rolling, and annealing procedures: one set with ~0.5 at% Hf addition and one control set without Hf. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and perform detailed microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM/TEM) to confirm the presence and distribution of Hf-rich precipitates.
measurements: Microstructural characteristics (precipitate size, distribution, and boundary coverage)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-added samples do not show a statistically significant increase in both strength and tensile ductility compared to the control, or if the microstructural analysis fails to reveal a uniform network of Hf-rich precipitates at or near the internal boundaries (or reveals detrimental effects such as embrittlement), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The strengthening effect of Hf on the alloy could be maintained at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.At different high temperatures, the Hf0.5 alloy exhibited a higher strength and ductility than the Hf0 alloys. The outstanding high-temperature strength of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the precipitation strengthening of the Hf-rich phase precipitated in the inner of the B2 phase. The excellent high-temperature ductility of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the pinning effect of the Hf-rich phase that existed at grain and phase boundaries to boundary sliding during the high-temperature deformation.
